stem: On 1 October each year a reservoir operator fixes how much storage to leave empty for the water year ahead. A group proposes four uses of 40 years of monthly fields from a climate-model ensemble, together with the basin's gauge record and the operator's own log. Which proposal is a supervised-ML problem for that decision, given the data each would use? Choose the best answer.
options: a) September's fields paired with the share of storage the operator left empty that year, so each year carries a number the log already holds · b) each water year's twelve months of fields paired with that year's gauged inflow, so the model learns from the months in which the inflow actually formed · c) September's fields paired with the water year's gauged inflow, so each year carries the volume that the months after the decision delivered · d) the ensemble's 40 water-year runoff totals and the gauge record's 40 inflows, pooled as two samples, to learn how far wet or dry the ensemble runs

stem: Each evening during a field campaign the flight planner decides whether to schedule the research aircraft for the next afternoon's convection. Four proposals would use three seasons of the campaign's evening soundings, its radar archive and its flight log. Which one can be set up as supervised ML for that decision? Choose the best answer.
options: a) each evening's sounding paired with whether the aircraft was scheduled for the next day, so every evening carries the call the planner made · b) each evening's sounding paired with the radar echo coverage of that same evening, so every evening carries a number the archive already holds · c) the next afternoon's sounding paired with that afternoon's convection, so the profile nearest the storms is what the model learns from · d) each evening's sounding paired with whether convection formed the next afternoon, so every evening carries the outcome the planner was weighing

stem: Four proposals: (1) predict next-day hail reports from 15 years of radar storm-cell attributes, 60,000 cells with a report flag; (2) classify 50,000 satellite scenes as cloud or clear from 8,000 analyst labels; (3) predict monthly streamflow from basin precipitation and temperature across 40 basins, 14,400 gauged months; (4) predict a grid cell's water-vapour mixing ratio from its specific humidity, 2 million cells. Which proposal should not be an ML project, and why? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the hail one — a report flag marks the cells someone reported, so the target is missing wherever nobody did and a model cannot learn toward it · b) the cloud one — a brightness-temperature threshold already sorts each scene into cloud or clear, so the analyst labels add nothing to learn · c) the streamflow one — fourteen thousand months over forty basins is 360 per basin, too few for a continuous target when basins differ · d) the mixing-ratio one — a one-line definition already turns specific humidity into mixing ratio, so a model would have nothing left to learn

stem: A review panel sees four proposals: (1) fill in the eastward and northward wind components on every level of an archived sounding set from the wind speed and direction already stored on that level, 1.2 million levels; (2) sort 80,000 lidar profiles into aerosol, cloud or clear using 4,000 analyst-labelled profiles; (3) estimate daily ozone at a monitor from 10 years of paired meteorology and readings, 3,650 days; (4) estimate a storm cell's chance of a tornado report from 15 years of cell attributes paired with reports, 90,000 cells. Which proposal should the panel send back as not an ML question, and on what reason? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the wind one — the components follow from speed and direction by plain trigonometry, so computing them settles it · b) the lidar one — a fixed backscatter threshold already separates the three classes, so there is nothing for the labels to teach · c) the ozone one — a monitor reading is a measurement rather than an outcome, so there is no target for a model to learn toward · d) the tornado one — reports are rare, so ninety thousand cells carry too few positive cases for a model to learn from

stem: A team's write-up lists five things that went wrong in one analysis, and a reviewer has written each one against a step of the spine. Which of the reviewer's pairings put the mistake with the step that exists to prevent it? Select all that apply; one mistake belongs to a step none of the pairings names.
options: a) validate — a setting was changed between runs and each run was judged on the cases it had learned from, so gains and memorising looked alike · b) test — the method was kept because it was the most elaborate one on the table, not because it scored better or cost less · c) train — the method that happened to run first became the method that shipped, and nothing else was ever run against it · d) justify — six months on nobody can rebuild the model, because the random seed and the chosen settings were not written down · e) test — the headline number comes from the cases the team consulted each time it adjusted a setting, right up to the end

stem: Five problems came up in a project review, and the reviewer has set each one against one of four steps. Which pairings put the problem with the step that guards against it? One problem belongs to a step the reviewer never names; select all that apply.
options: a) test — the configuration tried first was the one carried forward, and no second configuration was ever tried against it · b) train — nobody can reproduce the fit a year later, because which settings were chosen, and which seed, went unrecorded · c) validate — the number in the report was read off cases the team had already consulted each time it changed the model · d) justify — the model was picked for being the most advanced in the group rather than on measured performance and cost · e) test — each change to a setting was judged on the very cases the model had just learned from, so memorising passed as progress

stem: A team pools 2,000 member-years from a 50-member ensemble, shuffles them, and splits off a random fifth. On the other four-fifths it tunes a tree over several settings, scoring each on a slice of those four-fifths that was kept out of the fitting. It then scores the tuned tree once on the fifth and reports that as its expected skill on members it has never seen. What went wrong, and what does the reported number mean? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the tuning slice was reused for each setting tried, so the chosen settings fit those member-years and the number is too high for members never seen · b) the split drew member-years singly, so held-out years sit next to training years from the same run and the number is too high for members never seen · c) one pass over one random fifth is a single draw, so the number is too unsteady to quote for members never seen until averaged over several fifths · d) the shuffle before the split depends on the recorded seed, so the number quoted for members never seen would come out differently under another seed

stem: For a 40-member ensemble, each member-year carries the preceding autumn's fields and the winter precipitation of six Front Range basins. An analyst splits the record by basin, fitting on the three northern basins' member-years, tuning on a slice held out of the fitting rows, and scoring once on the three southern basins' rows for the same members and years. The result is written up as the skill to expect on a member the model has not met. What is the mistake, and what does that number tell the reader? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the southern basins are wetter than the northern ones, so the model's wet calls come true more often there and the number runs high for a member not yet met · b) holding a tuning slice out of the fitting rows left the model fitted on fewer rows than it had to work with, so its number runs low for a member not yet met · c) the split leaves each scored row sharing member and year with fitting rows, so each member it is scored on is one it has met and the number runs high for a member not yet met · d) the split was drawn by geography rather than by a random draw, so the number for a member not yet met depends on which basins happened to fall on which side

stem: A classifier for "wet winter" is scored on 100 held-out winters. Confusion matrix, rows = actual, columns = predicted — actual wet: 45 predicted wet, 15 predicted dry; actual dry: 30 predicted wet, 10 predicted dry. What are precision and recall for the wet class, to two decimals? Choose the best answer.
options: a) precision 0.60, recall 0.75 · b) precision 0.75, recall 0.60 · c) precision 0.45, recall 0.60 · d) precision 0.40, recall 0.25

Give, to the nearest hundredth, the hail class's precision and recall. Choose the best answer.
options: a) precision 0.80, recall 0.70 · b) precision 0.70, recall 0.80 · c) precision 0.23, recall 0.29 · d) precision 0.91, recall 0.86

stem: Logistic regression is the register's incumbent and gradient boosting a candidate trial. On the same member-grouped validation folds, logistic scores recall 0.72 / precision 0.70 and boosting 0.76 / 0.68. Over 20 paired fold scores, the corrected paired t-test on boosting minus logistic gives recall +0.04 (t = 2.31, p = 0.016) and precision −0.02 (t = −0.85, p = 0.797). The refinement budget is then spent. Which model does the register carry forward, and on what grounds? Choose the best answer.
options: a) boosting — recall's gain is measured at corrected p < 0.05, and one measured gain is what the validation folds exist to find · b) boosting — the precision drop fails to reach p < 0.05 on its own test, so it is noise and does not count against the measured recall gain · c) logistic — a candidate is promoted only when both numbers improve on average at corrected p < 0.05, and precision did not · d) logistic — recall is up at corrected p < 0.05, but precision fell on average, and the rule promotes only when the other number does not fall

stem: A decision tree is the model the register currently holds; gradient boosting is being tried against it. Scored on identical folds that hold out whole members, the tree reaches recall 0.81 / precision 0.77 and boosting 0.80 / 0.83. Across 24 paired fold scores, a Nadeau–Bengio corrected t-test of boosting minus the tree reads recall −0.01 (t = −0.52, p = 0.696) and precision +0.06 (t = 2.64, p = 0.007). The deadline ends the trials. Which model goes forward, and why? Choose the best answer.
options: a) boosting — precision is up at a corrected p well under 0.05, and a measured gain on either number is the result the trials were run to find · b) boosting — recall's dip is tiny and its own p of 0.304 is nowhere near 0.05, so the dip is noise and the precision gain carries the day · c) the tree — precision clears corrected p < 0.05, yet recall fell on average, and promotion needs the other number to hold or rise on average · d) the tree — a candidate goes forward only when recall and precision both rise on average and both clear p < 0.05, and recall did neither

stem: A small multilayer network is trained for 200 epochs on a two-class task, with two validation losses logged beside the training loss: one on a random fifth of the rows, drawn from every member, the other on four whole members held out. Epoch 20: training 0.62, random-rows 0.58, held-out members 0.60; epoch 50: 0.50, 0.44, 0.47; epoch 120: 0.31, 0.36, 0.52; epoch 200: 0.21, 0.38, 0.58. Which saved model should be carried into the comparison with the earlier tree and logistic models, and why? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the epoch-120 model — the random-rows validation loss reaches its minimum there, and with rows drawn across the members it is the larger and steadier sample of the two · b) the epoch-20 model — the two validation losses are closest to each other there, so the member effect has not yet set in and the fit is still honest · c) the epoch-50 model — the held-out-members validation loss reaches its minimum there, and those members are the cases the network has met in no year · d) the epoch-200 model — training loss is at its lowest there and the random-rows loss sits within a few hundredths of its minimum, so the fit has converged

stem: A network is trained for 300 epochs on storm-cell inputs for a hail-day task. The log carries the training loss and two validation losses: one on a random tenth of the days across the members, the other on three members kept out whole. Epoch 40: training 0.55, random-days 0.50, held-out members 0.52; epoch 140: 0.34, 0.30, 0.38; epoch 220: 0.19, 0.27, 0.45; epoch 300: 0.09, 0.29, 0.56. Which checkpoint goes forward to be compared against the tree and the logistic model built earlier, and on what reading of the curves? Choose the best answer.
options: a) epoch 140 — the loss on the held-out members bottoms out there, and they are the one part of the data the network did not fit · b) epoch 300 — a training loss of 0.09, with the random-days loss barely off its own minimum, shows the fit has converged · c) epoch 40 — the two validation losses sit closest together there, so the network has not yet begun to memorise its fitting members · d) epoch 220 — the random-days loss is at its minimum there, and because it samples each member it is the bigger of the two validation sets

stem: An attribution method is run on one prediction in which the network called a winter "wet". Contributions toward "wet": ENSO index +0.35; soil moisture −0.02; mid-tropospheric height pattern −0.10; snow cover +0.01. Which statement does this output support? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the ENSO index moved this one call toward "wet" because a high index makes winters wet, and the height pattern pulled back because ridges make them dry · b) the ENSO index moved this one call toward "wet" and the height pattern pulled it the other way, the first by more than the second · c) the network weighs the ENSO index more heavily than the height pattern whenever it calls a winter "wet", this call being one sample of that weighting · d) the +0.35 and the −0.10 are how far the ENSO index itself sat above its usual value that autumn and the height pattern below it, the first further

stem: On one prediction the network called a day "hail". Contributions toward "hail": mid-level lapse rate +0.28; low-level shear −0.12; storm-top height +0.06; freezing-level height −0.03; surface dewpoint +0.02. Which conclusion can be drawn from these numbers? Choose the best answer.
options: a) the +0.28 and the −0.12 say how far above its usual value the lapse rate was that day and how far below the shear was, the first by more · b) the network leans on the lapse rate more than on the shear whenever it calls a day "hail", and this one call is a sample of that leaning · c) the lapse rate pushed this one call toward "hail" because steep lapse rates make real hail likelier, and the shear pushed back because strong shear makes it rarer · d) the lapse rate pushed this one call toward "hail" and the shear pushed it the other way, with the lapse rate the larger of the two pushes

stem: An AI weather model such as NSF NCAR's CREDIT WXFormer needs far less computation at forecast time than a numerical model does. What produces the saving? Choose the best answer.
options: a) it steps forward with a function learned from past analyses, so at forecast time it does not solve the governing equations · b) it steps forward with the governing equations themselves, their coefficients learned from data, so it needs fewer iterations · c) it steps forward from a numerical model's own output, so it reuses the physics that model has run and skips the slow part · d) it steps forward from raw observations rather than from an analysis, so it does not wait for the assimilation a numerical run needs

stem: FourCastNet can turn out a 10-day global forecast far faster than a numerical model can. Which statement explains how it manages that? Choose the best answer.
options: a) it was trained on station and satellite observations, not on analyses, so no assimilation has to finish before it starts · b) a network trained on past analyses produces each next state directly, so no physics is solved along the way · c) it is a network fitted to past numerical forecasts, so it inherits their physics and only has to correct them · d) it feeds its own output back in but integrates the same equations with a coarser learned step, reaching day 10 sooner

stem: A forecaster has a 10-day run from an AI weather model for a tropical cyclone, and four facts about the run. Select all that apply: in which TWO of them does the output need a check against a numerical model or observations before it is used?
options: a) the run's day-5 track error so far is larger than the scorecard's mean day-5 error, at a lead time the scorecard covers · b) the run's day-9 intensity is higher than that of the strongest cyclone anywhere in the years the model was trained on · c) the run's day-5 intensity sits among the strongest 5 % of the storms in the years the model was trained on, though not above them · d) day 6 is inside the lead times the scorecard covers, but the scorecard was built from runs started from another centre's analysis

stem: An AI weather model's run for a June heat event over the Front Range arrives with four notes attached. Select all that apply — the TWO notes that mean its output cannot be used until it is checked against observations or a numerical run.
options: a) the forecast ridge over the region is stronger than the strongest ridge found in the model's training years, by a clear margin · b) Denver's day-3 high came in 2 °C warmer than the run forecast it, a miss bigger than the day-3 error the scorecard reports on average · c) the chart shows day 6, inside the scorecard's range, but the scorecard was compiled for a previous version of the network, not this run's · d) the day-4 850-hPa temperature anomaly over Denver ranks in the warmest 5 % of the summers in the model's training record, not above them
